entries.title: US copyright needs a human author, and the courts have said so
entries.take: In the US, a work with no human author cannot be registered, and the Supreme Court declined in March 2026 to revisit that.
entries.body: The D.C. Circuit decided Thaler v. Perlmutter (No. 23-5233) on 18 March 2025. It held that the Copyright Act requires eligible work to be authored first by a human being, and it upheld the refusal to register an image credited to a software system. The Supreme Court's docket for No. 25-449 shows the petition denied on 2 March 2026. The case concerned an image, not a song, and it did not say how much human input is enough.
do: Treat a track made by a tool with no real human input from you as outside US copyright protection.
Ask a music lawyer how the rule applies if your human input is partial.

entries.title: A text prompt alone does not make you the author of the output
entries.take: The Copyright Office says that, with today's tools, prompts alone do not give a user enough control to be the author of what comes back.
entries.body: Part 2 of the Office's AI report (29 January 2025) says human authors keep rights in what they wrote or played that shows in an output, in a creative selection or arrangement of outputs, and in creative changes they make. Whether the human input is enough is decided case by case. The Office saw no need for a new right for AI-generated content. This is the Office's view, not a court ruling.
do: Keep dated project files that show what you wrote, played and edited yourself.
Treat a song generated from a prompt alone as unprotected in the US.

entries.title: Registering a song that contains AI material with the US Copyright Office
entries.take: Use the Standard Application, claim only your own authorship, and exclude AI material that is more than a minor part of the work.
entries.body: The Office's guidance (88 FR 16190, effective 16 March 2023) says to describe the human authorship in the Author Created field and not to name an AI tool or its maker as an author. AI content beyond a minor amount should be excluded, which can be done under Limitation of the Claim, Other, Material Excluded. If you are unsure, you can give a general statement that the work contains AI material, and the Office will follow up. An earlier registration can be corrected by a supplementary registration. The guidance covers all kinds of works and does not name music.
do: Describe your own contribution in the Author Created field.
List the AI-generated material as excluded in Limitation of the Claim.
Ask a music lawyer before filing if ownership of the AI output is unclear.

entries.title: UK law still protects computer-generated works, but the government proposes ending that
entries.take: Section 9(3) of the UK Act names the person who arranged a computer-generated work as its author; the March 2026 report proposes removing that rule.
entries.body: The report of 18 March 2026 says section 9(3) CDPA sits uneasily with the originality test, and proposes removing the protection for works generated wholly by a computer unless evidence shows ongoing value. Works made with AI help that still show human creativity would stay protected. The report adds that AI-generated music may still be covered as a sound recording. This is a proposal, not a change in the law.

entries.title: The Copyright Office's training report exists only as a pre-publication version
entries.take: Part 3 calls training an audio model to make new recordings for the same market at best modestly transformative, and leaves fair use to case-by-case decisions.
entries.body: The Office released Part 3 in pre-publication form on 9 May 2025, and its AI page, checked 20 November 2026, still says a final version will follow with no substantive change expected. The report says training an audio model on recordings to generate new recordings aims at the same market, while using a model to remove unwanted distortion would be more transformative. It says existing or likely licence markets weigh against fair use, and that government intervention in licensing would be premature. It is the Office's view and does not bind courts.

entries.title: In the EU, rightsholders can reserve their music from commercial text and data mining
entries.take: In the EU, commercial text and data mining of lawfully accessible works is allowed unless the rightsholder reserves the use; German law requires online reservations to be machine-readable.
entries.body: GEMA's notice explains the rule as Germany applies it in section 44b UrhG, which implements Article 4 of the EU copyright directive of 2019. GEMA says it declared the reservation for the works it represents, including for uses outside Germany, and that licensees who put its repertoire online must signal the reservation in machine-readable form. GEMA's own notice adds that it is not settled whether commercial generative AI falls under the exception. German court rulings on this are in the litigation entries.
do: Check whether your society has filed a reservation covering your works.
Ask a music lawyer how a reservation applies to music you publish yourself.

entries.title: EU rules make AI model providers keep a copyright policy and publish a training summary
entries.take: In the EU, general-purpose AI model providers must keep a copyright policy and publish a training summary; Commission enforcement, with fines, began on 2 August 2026.
entries.body: The Commission says the duties applied from 2 August 2025, its enforcement powers apply from 2 August 2026, and models placed on the market earlier must comply by 2 August 2027. The two public duties are a policy to respect EU copyright, including rights reservations, and a published summary of what content it trained on, for which the Commission published a template (24 July 2025, updated 26 March 2026). The voluntary Code of Practice of 10 July 2025 has a copyright chapter. The summary gives rightsholders something to read; it is not a licence.

entries.title: Text and data mining (TDM)
entries.take: Automated analysis of one or more digital works to extract information such as patterns, trends and correlations. In the EU, a commercial use is allowed only where the rightsholder has not reserved it.

entries.title: Training content summary
entries.take: The overview of what content trained a general-purpose AI model, which EU rules require its provider to publish in the Commission's template format.

entries.title: Digital replica
entries.take: In the NO FAKES bill (S. 4591, not law as of November 2026), a newly made, computer-generated, highly realistic copy of a person's voice or likeness. Authorised remixes, samples and remasters are excluded.

entries.title: Tennessee's ELVIS Act protects a person's voice, including a simulated one
entries.take: Since 1 July 2024, Tennessee law covers a voice whether real or simulated, and reaches tools whose main purpose is copying one person's voice.
entries.body: Public Chapter 588 (HB 2091) amends Tennessee's personal rights law. It defines voice as a sound readily identifiable with an individual, real or simulated. It creates liability for publishing or distributing a voice or likeness with knowledge it was not authorised, and for offering a tool whose primary purpose is producing a specific person's voice or likeness. A company holding an exclusive recording or distribution contract can also sue. Uses such as news, criticism and parody are treated as fair where the First Amendment protects them. It is state law; a lawyer should say whether it reaches a case.

entries.title: California and New York have signed performer digital replica laws
entries.take: Governors signed California bills on 17 September 2024 and New York bills on 11 December 2025; read the statute text before relying on a summary.
entries.body: California's governor describes AB 2602 (contracts must say when an AI replica of a performer's voice or likeness will be used, and the performer needs professional representation in the deal) and AB 1836 (no commercial use of a deceased performer's digital replica without estate consent). New York's governor describes S.8420-A (advertisers must identify AI synthetic performers) and S.8391 (heirs or executors must consent to commercial use of a dead person's name, image or likeness). These are the governors' summaries; check each statute's text and start date, with a music lawyer, before relying on it.

entries.title: The NO FAKES Act has cleared a Senate committee but is not law
entries.take: S. 4591 is a bill, not law. It was reported to the Senate on 24 June 2026 (Calendar No. 446); no Senate or House vote was found as of 20 November 2026.
entries.body: Sen. Coons introduced S. 4591 on 20 May 2026 with Sen. Blackburn, Sen. Klobuchar and others. The Judiciary Committee advanced it unanimously, per the sponsors' release of 18 June 2026, and Sen. Grassley reported it with an amendment on 24 June. The release mentions a House companion. Congress.gov blocks automated reading, and on 20 November 2026 govinfo held only the introduced and reported texts. Until a bill is passed and signed, it changes nothing.
do: Check congress.gov for S. 4591 before relying on this status.

entries.title: What the reported NO FAKES text would do for a voice or likeness
entries.take: The reported bill would create a federal property right in voice and visual likeness, with limits on licence length and a takedown process for platforms.
entries.body: The reported text makes the right licensable but not assignable during life, limits a lifetime licence to 10 years, and lets the right run after death for up to 70 years through renewals. Platforms would act on notices, with a counter-notice step of at least 14 days before restoring material. It would take effect 180 days after enactment. It also contains a preemption section with carve-outs, including state laws in place on 2 January 2025. Details can change before passage. A music lawyer should read the text for any real decision.

entries.title: Mistake: signing a long or total voice and likeness licence without a music lawyer
entries.take: A broad licence of your voice or likeness can leave you without control for years; both the Copyright Office and the NO FAKES text point to that risk.
entries.body: Part 1 of the Copyright Office's report (31 July 2024) recommends that people may license their voice and image but not fully assign them, and warns that unequal bargaining power, especially early in a career, can lock people into broad terms. The reported NO FAKES text would cap a lifetime licence at 10 years. Neither is current law for your contract. What a deal covers, for how long and for which uses is a contract question.
do: Have a music lawyer read any AI voice or likeness licence before you agree.
Ask what is licensed, for how long, and whether you can end it.

entries.title: Mistake: releasing a voice clone of a real artist without their approval
entries.take: Spotify allows vocal impersonation only with the impersonated artist's authorisation, and Tennessee law can reach unauthorised voice use.
entries.body: Spotify's September 2025 policy says vocal impersonation is allowed in music on its service only when the artist whose voice is imitated has authorised it. Tennessee's ELVIS Act, in force since 1 July 2024, covers real or simulated voices. Other places have other rules. A track that imitates a named artist's voice without approval breaks Spotify's policy, and the artist may also have a legal claim. A music lawyer can advise on a specific case.
do: Get written approval from an artist before releasing a model of their voice.
Use your own voice or a licensed voice model.

entries.title: In Germany, a court ruled for GEMA against OpenAI over song lyrics
entries.take: Munich Regional Court I ruled for GEMA on 11 November 2025 (42 O 14139/24); LTO reported it was not yet final.
entries.body: Per GEMA, the court held that OpenAI should have licensed lyrics in GEMA's repertoire for training and running ChatGPT, that the systems hold copies reproduced in response to simple prompts, and that the text and data mining exception does not justify storing or outputting them. LTO gives the docket and says nine songs were at issue. GEMA is a party, so its account is one side's. This is one first-instance German court on lyrics, not music audio. No appeal docket was confirmed in the pages opened.

entries.title: In Germany, a court largely upheld GEMA's claims against Suno
entries.take: Per the court's own release, Munich Regional Court I largely upheld GEMA's claims against Suno on 31 July 2026 (42 O 763/25); the judgment is not final.
entries.body: The 42nd civil chamber ruled on six musical works, not lyrics. It found the works reproducibly contained in Suno models v3.5 and v4 stored on servers in Germany, held that this copy was not covered by the text and data mining exception, and found the outputs infringed. It held Suno, not its users, responsible for outputs from simple prompts. It also upheld claims for copying during training in the US and rejected fair use. Suno disputed the claims at the hearing of 9 March 2026. This is a first-instance ruling in one court, and no appeal decision was found.

entries.title: UMG and Sony v Suno: two US cases, each an allegation so far
entries.take: UMG and Sony's claims against Suno in D. Mass. are allegations; Suno's answer of 1 September 2026 admits it trained on audio data taken from YouTube.
entries.body: In 1:24-cv-11611-FDS, the labels filed a first amended complaint on 25 August 2026 (Dkt. 277) alleging copying of audio from YouTube and getting around its access controls. Suno answered on 1 September 2026 (Dkt. 281), admitting it used audio data taken from YouTube as training data and denying much of the rest. A second action, 1:26-cv-14275, filed on 18 September 2026, asserts 60,202 recordings and targets Suno's v6 model. The latest step opened was 18 September 2026; no ruling on the merits was found.

entries.title: Sony v Udio: two New York cases, and UMG settled
entries.take: Sony's claims against Udio (S.D.N.Y.) are allegations; Udio's answer of 27 August 2026 admits it trained on audio data taken from YouTube.
entries.body: Sony's first case against Uncharted Labs (Udio) is 1:24-cv-04777 (AKH), filed 24 June 2024 per its later complaint. A second, 1:26-cv-6120, was filed on 20 July 2026 and asserts 30,117 recordings. Udio's answer in the second case (Dkt. 25, 27 August 2026) admits it used audio data taken from YouTube as training data. UMG announced a settlement and licences with Udio on 30 October 2025. The latest step opened was 27 August 2026; no ruling on the merits was found.

entries.title: Concord v Anthropic: the publishers moved to drop two claims in April 2026
entries.take: In the first lyrics case against Anthropic, the publishers filed notice on 20 April 2026 dropping two secondary-liability claims with prejudice; a second case is pending.
entries.body: In Concord Music Group v. Anthropic (N.D. Cal., 5:24-cv-03811-EKL-SVK, Judge Eumi K. Lee), the publishers filed a notice dropping Counts II and III, contributory and vicarious infringement (Dkt. 685, 20 April 2026); it says Anthropic had not agreed to a stipulation. Music Business Worldwide reports a second suit filed in January 2026 and Anthropic motions to dismiss part of it, filed 3 August 2026 and set for hearing on 4 November 2026. No ruling on those motions was found. These are allegations and arguments, not findings.

entries.title: Independent artists have proposed class actions against Suno and Udio
entries.take: Trade press reports Justice v Suno largely survived a motion to dismiss on 20 August 2026, and Woulard v Udio moved to New York on 3 August 2026.
entries.body: Music Business Worldwide reports that Judge Saylor (D. Mass.) denied Suno's motion on two of three challenged counts on 20 August 2026, leaving output and YouTube-circumvention claims, and dismissed one count the plaintiffs had cited by mistake. It reports that Judge Ellis (N.D. Ill.) transferred Woulard v Udio to the Southern District of New York on 3 August 2026, without prejudice to Udio refiling its motion. Both are proposed class actions with unproven allegations.

entries.title: SOCAN says it has sued Suno over 150 outputs
entries.take: SOCAN sued Suno in the Federal Court of Canada (T-3803-26) over a sample of 150 outputs; it says Suno has neither a licence nor paid it. The claims are unproven.
entries.body: SOCAN's statement of claim was issued on 2 September 2026 and amended on 18 November 2026. SOCAN's page says the claim lists 150 publicly available Suno outputs that it says replicate songs in its repertoire, and that making them available in Canada infringed its performing rights. It says SOCAN has issued no licence to Suno and received no payment. SOCAN is a party, so its page gives one side. No defence or ruling was found.

entries.title: Labels and publishers have licensed AI music firms since October 2025
entries.take: UMG, Merlin, Warner, Kobalt and BMG have announced AI deals; none of the sources opened gives money terms, and some rest on trade reports.
entries.body: UMG and Udio announced a settlement and licences on 30 October 2025 (UMG release). Merlin and Udio announced a licensing framework on 20 January 2026 for participating members. Music Business Worldwide reports Warner and Suno on 25 November 2025 and Kobalt and Udio on 9 April 2026, the latter with opt-in voices and compositions. BMG's parent posted a BMG and Suno alliance on 14 August 2026 (MBW dates the deal 12 August) where artists and writers choose to take part. No financial terms were published in these sources.
do: Ask your label, publisher or distributor if your catalogue is included and how to opt in or out.

entries.title: GEMA's AI licence model asks for 30 percent of a provider's net income
entries.take: GEMA's two-part licence model, set out in September 2024, asks AI providers for a 30 percent share of net income, with a minimum royalty tied to output.
entries.body: GEMA says the first component covers training, including fine-tuning, with 30 percent of the net income of the model or system and a minimum royalty linked to how much output is produced. It targets providers operating in the German market whatever the place of training. A second component would cover later use of AI-generated music, such as background music. This is GEMA's own proposed model. The sources opened do not name a provider that has signed it.

entries.title: Sweden's STIM announced a collective AI licence in September 2025
entries.take: CISAC reported on 9 September 2025 that STIM signed what it called the first collective AI licence, with attribution technology built in.
entries.body: CISAC's report names Songfox as the first company under the licence and Sureel as the attribution provider, so outputs can be traced to the works that influenced them. Pay is described as flowing from training and from later use of outputs. The framework is open to AI firms that meet STIM's criteria, and the launch repertoire was deliberately limited. No rates are given on the page. Sweden is outside this guide's covered territories; it is here as a model.

entries.title: SOCAN named Musical AI an approved attribution partner
entries.take: SOCAN's release of 20 July 2026 sets opt-in and credit-and-compensation principles; it gives no rates or payout terms.
entries.body: SOCAN says Musical AI will be its approved partner for attribution work, and the two will explore guidelines for attribution technology in Canada. The release rests on two principles: any AI use of a creator's work should be opt-in, and a creator should be credited and paid when the work shapes an output. No rates, payout method or launch date for member tools appear in the release. SOCAN's separate claim against Suno is covered in the litigation entries.

entries.title: EU AI-content labelling duties apply from 2 August 2026
entries.take: In the EU, AI Act transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, and a voluntary code on marking and labelling AI content was finalised on 10 June 2026.
entries.body: The Commission says the code helps providers and deployers of generative AI meet the transparency duties. From 2 August 2026 clear labelling is required in key cases: deepfakes, AI text about public-interest topics, and telling users when they deal with an AI system. Generators already on the market before that date have until 2 December 2026 for machine-readable marking (see the next entry). The page does not mention music by name. Whether a given AI song needs a label depends on the legal text and the facts, so ask a music lawyer.

entries.title: In the EU, AI generators already on sale have until 2 December 2026 to mark outputs
entries.take: In the EU, AI systems generating synthetic audio and placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking duty by 2 December 2026.
entries.body: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on the third day after. It adds Article 111(4) to the AI Act: providers of AI systems, including general-purpose ones, that generate synthetic audio, images, video or text and were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with the Article 50(2) marking duty by 2 December 2026. Systems placed on the market later have no such extra time.

entries.title: The UK dropped the opt-out data mining exception as its preferred route
entries.take: The UK government's report of 18 March 2026 no longer prefers a wide data mining exception with an opt-out, and says it will not reform copyright until it is confident.
entries.body: The report was published on 18 March 2026 with an impact assessment. It proposes gathering more evidence, watching transparency rules abroad and working on best practice for AI transparency. It notes the UK has no duty to label AI-generated content and proposes work with industry on labelling. It also proposes exploring options on digital replicas, including whether a new right would help. Nothing in it changes UK law yet. This guide treats the UK separately from the EU.

entries.title: Spotify's AI policy: no unauthorised voice clones, a spam filter and AI credits
entries.take: Spotify's post of 25 September 2025 bars vocal impersonation without the artist's approval and backs AI credits delivered through DDEX.
entries.body: Spotify says it took down more than 75 million spam tracks in the previous 12 months and would roll out a spam filter conservatively. AI credits come from labels, distributors and partners. An update on the same page says a beta launched on 16 April that shows AI credits in Song Credits on mobile where artists chose to disclose, and that a missing credit does not mean AI was not used. The update gives no year; it calls the first post last fall, which points to 2026.
do: Ask your distributor whether it can deliver AI credits to Spotify.

entries.title: Deezer says AI tracks passed 50 percent of daily uploads at the June 2026 peak
entries.unit: percent of new uploads at the June 2026 peak
entries.take: Deezer's own detector count: about 90,000 fully AI tracks a day, not independently checked. The release dates its first AI tagging to both June 2025 and June 2026.

entries.title: Deezer says fully AI tracks are 1 to 3 percent of its streams
entries.take: Deezer's own figure, as of June 2026. It excludes detected AI tracks from recommendations and says up to 85% of their 2025 streams were fraudulent.

entries.title: YouTube requires disclosure of realistic AI content and offers face likeness detection
entries.take: YouTube requires creators to disclose realistic AI-made content, including music that is the main focus of a video; its likeness tool described matches faces.
entries.body: The YouTube Help page says creators disclose realistic AI-generated or meaningfully altered content in YouTube Studio, and lists music that is the main focus of a video among the examples. Non-realistic content and minor edits need no disclosure. Creators who keep failing to disclose may get a label added or face penalties. YouTube's blog of 21 April 2026 says likeness detection is offered to talent agencies, management companies and the people they represent, and describes matching faces. Voice detection was not described on the pages opened.

entries.title: Apple Music's AI tags depend on what labels and distributors declare
entries.take: Music Business Worldwide reports Apple's four AI transparency tags rely on suppliers; CD Baby says it is working on AI credits with Spotify.
entries.body: Per Music Business Worldwide, Apple told partners on 4 March 2026 about tags for artwork, track, composition and music video, which labels and distributors can use now and will have to use for new deliveries later; the specification calls them optional for now. Apple defers to suppliers on what counts as AI-generated. CD Baby's blog of 1 October 2025 says it is working with Spotify and partners on a standard for AI credits in metadata. Ask your own distributor how it handles AI.
do: Answer your distributor's AI question on the upload form as it is asked.

entries.title: DDEX ERN 4.3.1 can mark a recording or contribution as made by generative AI
entries.take: Version 4.3.1 of the DDEX release message adds ways to say a recording, or one contribution, was made fully or partly by a generative AI tool.
entries.body: The release notes in DDEX's ERN standard list the two additions for version 4.3.1; the current version, 4.3.2, keeps them. These messages are what labels and distributors send to services, so the flag reaches a platform only if your distributor collects the answer and delivers it. The exact element names were not checked. Spotify's post says its AI credits standard is developed through DDEX, and the UK report notes DDEX work on metadata for AI-generated music.
do: Ask your distributor or label which AI fields it sends to each service.

entries.title: ASCAP, BMI and SOCAN accept partly AI works and reject wholly AI ones
entries.take: On 28 October 2025 the three societies aligned: works that combine AI material with human authorship can be registered, entirely AI-made works cannot.
entries.body: This rests on SOCAN's pages; check ASCAP's and BMI's own pages too. SOCAN separates AI-generated outputs, which it will not register and may remove, from AI-assisted works, which it will. It says members need not explain their AI use at registration for an AI-assisted work, and that the member carries responsibility for registrations. If you registered a wholly AI output by mistake, SOCAN asks you to contact it to have it removed.
do: Read your society's AI policy before you register an AI-assisted song.
Ask your society to remove any wholly AI work you registered by mistake.

entries.title: The MLC will not register wholly AI works and does not judge individual songs
entries.take: The MLC follows Copyright Office guidance, cannot register entirely AI-generated works and does not decide whether a given song has enough human authorship.
entries.body: The MLC's help article says works with meaningful human authorship may be registered and entirely AI-generated works may not. It says it does not assess individual works and points members to Copyright Office guidance or counsel. In a 2023 letter the Copyright Office told the MLC it may hold royalties on a work that seems to have no human author while it investigates, with an adjustment dispute route for the claimant.
do: Keep records of your own authorship in case the MLC asks about a work.

entries.title: GEMA's work form has a box confirming the work was not made only by AI
entries.take: GEMA's online work registration has a tick box confirming the work was not made only by AI, added as part of its anti-fraud work.
entries.body: GEMA's help page says the box aims to stop payments for content that took no creative work. The page's wording conflicts: the box confirms the work was not made only by AI, but the next line says to tick it where the work was made entirely or partly without AI. Either way, a wholly AI-generated work cannot be confirmed as the member's own. Ask GEMA if you are unsure how your process fits.
do: Tick the box only if AI was not the sole creator of the work.

entries.title: AI-assisted work and AI-generated output
entries.take: SOCAN's split: an AI-assisted work is made by a person using AI as a tool; an AI-generated output is made with minimal human involvement and cannot be registered.

entries.title: If you use AI in your music
entries.take: A working list for a songwriter, artist, producer or admin who uses AI tools. It is not legal advice; ask a music lawyer about contracts.

groups.name: Before you start
items: Read the tool's terms on who owns outputs and whether your inputs train its models.
Decide which parts you will write, play or edit yourself.
Do not feed in someone else's recording, lyrics or voice without permission.

groups.name: While you work
items: Keep dated project files, stems and notes that show your own contribution.
Save the prompts and settings behind each AI-made element.
Note which tool and version produced each AI element.

groups.name: Before you release
items: Answer your distributor's AI question as it is asked.
Add AI credits where your distributor and the service support them.
Avoid a voice that imitates a named artist unless they approved.

groups.name: Before you register
items: Register only works that carry your own authorship.
In the US, use the Standard Application and describe the AI material.
Answer your society's AI question truthfully, for example GEMA's box.
Know that ASCAP, BMI, SOCAN and the MLC do not register wholly AI works.

groups.name: If a voice or likeness is involved
items: Get written permission from the person before using a model of their voice.
Have a music lawyer read any voice or likeness licence.

usco-part2.support: Executive summary bullets: prompts alone not enough control; human contributions, selection, arrangement and modification protectable; case by case.

fr-2023-05321.title: Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence, 88 FR 16190
fr-2023-05321.support: Standard Application; describe human authorship; exclude AI content above de minimis under Limitation of the Claim; supplementary registration to correct.

socan-ai-guidelines.support: AI-generated outputs cannot be registered; AI-assisted works can; no disclosure of how AI was used needed; member responsible; removal.

mlc-ai-help.title: Can I register an AI-generated work with The MLC?
mlc-ai-help.support: Help article: follows Copyright Office guidance; entirely AI-generated works cannot be registered; meaningful human authorship can; the MLC does not assess individual works.

usco-mlc-letter.title: Letter to The MLC: Royalty Eligibility of Musical Works Generated Using Artificial Intelligence
usco-mlc-letter.support: Works lacking human authorship have no copyright owner and earn no blanket licence royalty; the collective may hold royalties pending an investigation; adjustment dispute route.

gema-ai-declaration.title: Why do I have to confirm during the work declaration process that my work was not created exclusively by AI?
gema-ai-declaration.support: Help page: AI checkbox in online work registration, introduced under its anti-fraud campaign.

uk-ai-copyright-report.publisher: UK Government (DSIT, DCMS and Intellectual Property Office)
uk-ai-copyright-report.title: Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
uk-ai-copyright-report.support: Opt-out exception no longer preferred; no reform until confident; no UK labelling duty; proposes removing s.9(3) CDPA protection; AI music may stay protected as sound recordings; digital replica options; DDEX metadata work.

usco-part3.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training (pre-publication version)

usco-ai-hub.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (initiative hub)
usco-ai-hub.support: Hub lists Part 1 (31 Jul 2024), Part 2 (29 Jan 2025) and Part 3 pre-publication (9 May 2025); final Part 3 still described as future.

gema-tdm.title: Website Text- und Datamining Rechtevorbehaltserklärung (rights reservation notice)
gema-tdm.support: GEMA says it declared the reservation under section 44b(3) UrhG for its repertoire, including uses outside Germany; licensees must signal it machine-readably; quotes Art. 4 DSM Directive.

eu-gpai-guidelines.title: Guidelines for providers of general-purpose AI models
eu-gpai-guidelines.support: Obligations apply from 2 Aug 2025; enforcement powers from 2 Aug 2026; models placed before 2 Aug 2025 comply by 2 Aug 2027.

eu-gpai-qa.title: Guidelines on obligations for general-purpose AI providers (Q&A)
eu-gpai-qa.support: Two public duties for all GPAI providers: a copyright policy respecting rights reservations, and a public summary of training content.

eu-gpai-code.title: The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
eu-gpai-code.support: Voluntary code published 10 Jul 2025 with Transparency, Copyright and Safety chapters.

eu-training-template.title: Explanatory Notice and Template for the Public Summary of Training Content for general-purpose AI models
eu-training-template.support: Template described as a common minimal baseline; page shows publication 24 Jul 2025 and last update 26 Mar 2026.

s4591-rs.title: S. 4591, NO FAKES Act of 2026, reported in the Senate (Calendar No. 446)
s4591-rs.support: Introduced 20 May 2026; reported 24 Jun 2026 with an amendment; definitions, rights, licence limits, safe harbours, preemption and effective date sections.

elvis-act.title: Public Chapter 588, House Bill 2091 (Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act of 2024)
elvis-act.support: Defines voice incl. simulation; liability for unauthorised publication and for tools whose primary purpose is a specific individual's voice; takes effect 1 Jul 2024.

ca-gov-2024.publisher: Office of the Governor of California
ca-gov-2024.title: Governor Newsom signs bills to protect digital likeness of performers
ca-gov-2024.support: Describes AB 2602 (contracts, professional representation) and AB 1836 (deceased performers, estate consent).

ny-gov-2025.publisher: Office of the Governor of New York
ny-gov-2025.title: Governor Hochul signs legislation to protect consumers and boost AI transparency in the film industry
ny-gov-2025.support: Describes S.8420-A/A.8887-B (AI synthetic performer disclosure in ads) and S.8391/A.8882 (post-mortem consent).

blackburn-nofakes.title: Blackburn, Coons bipartisan bill to protect individuals and creators from deepfakes passes Senate Judiciary Committee
blackburn-nofakes.support: Sponsors' release of 18 Jun 2026: bill advanced unanimously out of committee; House companion by Reps. Salazar and Dean; revised version introduced the month before.

usco-part1.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 1: Digital Replicas
usco-part1.support: Recommends a federal digital replica law; recommends individuals may license but not fully assign voice and image; warns about unequal bargaining power.

spotify-ai-2025.title: Spotify strengthens AI protections for artists, songwriters, and producers
spotify-ai-2025.support: Spotify's own policy: impersonation allowed only with the artist's authorisation; spam filter; DDEX-based AI credits. Undated update: beta of AI credits launched 16 April (no year given).

gema-openai.title: Europe's first landmark ruling on AI: GEMA prevails against OpenAI
gema-openai.support: GEMA's own account of the 11 Nov 2025 ruling; mentions its licensing model from Sept 2024. A party account, not the judgment.

lto-gema-openai.title: GEMA siegt gegen OpenAI im Streit um Liedtexte
lto-gema-openai.support: Gives docket 42 O 14139/24, nine songs, judgment of 11 Nov 2025, not yet final.

lg-munich-suno.publisher: Landgericht München I, press office (published by the Bavarian Ministry of Justice)
lg-munich-suno.title: Pressemitteilung 16: Urteil GEMA gegen SUNO
lg-munich-suno.support: Court press release on the 31 Jul 2026 judgment, 42 O 763/25: claims largely upheld, six works, memorisation, outputs, TDM exception, not final.
lg-munich-suno.court: Landgericht München I (Munich Regional Court I), 42nd civil chamber

lg-munich-suno-hearing.publisher: Landgericht München I, press office (published by the Bavarian Ministry of Justice)
lg-munich-suno-hearing.title: Pressemitteilung 6: Verhandlung GEMA gegen Suno Inc.
lg-munich-suno-hearing.support: Court press release on the hearing of 9 Mar 2026 in 42 O 763/25.
lg-munich-suno-hearing.court: Landgericht München I (Munich Regional Court I), 42nd civil chamber

mad-suno-fac.publisher: Plaintiffs UMG Recordings, Capitol Records and Sony Music Entertainment (filed in D. Mass.)
mad-suno-fac.title: UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Suno, Inc., First Amended Complaint (Dkt. 277)
mad-suno-fac.support: Plaintiffs' amended pleading filed 25 Aug 2026 alleging stream ripping from YouTube and circumvention of its rolling cipher. Copy hosted by a trade site; allegations only.

mad-suno-answer.publisher: Defendant Suno, Inc. (filed in D. Mass.)
mad-suno-answer.title: UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Suno, Inc., Suno's answer (Dkt. 281)
mad-suno-answer.support: Suno's answer filed 1 Sep 2026, para. 7: admits it obtained audio data from YouTube for use as training data; denies the rest of that paragraph. Copy hosted by a trade site.

mad-suno-second.publisher: Plaintiffs UMG, Capitol, Sony Music Entertainment and Sony labels (filed in D. Mass.)
mad-suno-second.title: UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Suno, Inc., Complaint (Dkt. 1), second action
mad-suno-second.support: Second action complaint dated 18 Sep 2026: 60,202 recordings; refers to the v6 model released 9 Sep 2026. Allegations only.

nysd-udio-second.publisher: Plaintiffs Sony Music Entertainment and Sony labels (filed in S.D.N.Y.)
nysd-udio-second.title: Sony Music Entertainment v. Uncharted Labs, Inc. (Udio), Complaint, second action
nysd-udio-second.support: Complaint filed 20 Jul 2026 (date per Udio's answer) asserting 30,117 recordings; cites the first action 1:24-cv-04777 (AKH), filed 24 Jun 2024. Allegations only.

nysd-udio-answer.publisher: Defendant Uncharted Labs, Inc. d/b/a Udio.com (filed in S.D.N.Y.)
nysd-udio-answer.title: Sony Music Entertainment v. Uncharted Labs, Inc., Udio's answer (Dkt. 25)
nysd-udio-answer.support: Udio's answer filed 27 Aug 2026 in 1:26-cv-06120-AKH; admits it obtained audio data from YouTube for use as training data. Copy hosted by a trade site.

umg-udio-release.publisher: Universal Music Group and Udio (via PR Newswire)
umg-udio-release.title: Universal Music Group and Udio announce Udio's first strategic agreements for new licensed AI music creation platform
umg-udio-release.support: Company release: settlement plus recorded and publishing licences; new platform in 2026; no figures given.

cand-concord-685.publisher: Plaintiff publishers (Concord Music Group, Inc. et al.), filed in N.D. Cal.
cand-concord-685.title: Concord Music Group, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC, Publishers' notice of voluntary dismissal of Counts II and III with prejudice (Dkt. 685)
cand-concord-685.support: Notice filed 20 Apr 2026 dismissing Counts II (contributory) and III (vicarious) with prejudice; footnote 1 says Anthropic had declined to stipulate and the publishers may seek leave to amend.

mbw-concord-two.title: Anthropic seeks partial dismissal in music publishers' $3B lyrics suit, as CEO moves to drop the direct-infringement claim against him
mbw-concord-two.support: Trade report: second suit filed Jan 2026; motions to dismiss filed 3 Aug 2026; hearing set 4 Nov 2026; mentions settlements and deals.

mbw-justice-suno.title: Judge refuses to dismiss indie artist's proposed class action against Suno, clearing AI output and stream-ripping claims for discovery
mbw-justice-suno.support: Trade report of an order of 20 Aug 2026 (Judge Saylor, D. Mass.): two challenged counts survive, one falls.

mbw-woulard-udio.title: Court declines to dismiss independent artists' copyright class action against Udio, but moves the case from Illinois to New York
mbw-woulard-udio.support: Trade report of an order of 3 Aug 2026 (Judge Ellis, N.D. Ill.): transferred to S.D.N.Y., motion to dismiss denied without prejudice.

socan-suno.title: Innovation Must Respect Human Creativity (SOCAN v. Suno)
socan-suno.support: SOCAN's page on its claim: 150-output sample, no licence or payment from Suno, performing-rights allegation; links the statement of claim.

eu-marking-code.title: Commission publishes Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
eu-marking-code.support: Final voluntary code; transparency obligations apply from 2 Aug 2026; page updated 12 Jun 2026.

merlin-udio.title: Merlin and Udio partner to advance AI for independent music
merlin-udio.support: Licensing framework for participating Merlin members' repertoire to train AI models; no financial terms given.

bmg-suno.title: BMG and Suno forge AI music alliance
bmg-suno.support: Bertelsmann news item dated 14 Aug 2026: global BMG and Suno alliance covering recordings and publishing; participating artists and songwriters opt in; settles prior use; no terms given.

mbw-wmg-suno.title: Warner Music Group strikes 'landmark' deal with Suno; settles copyright lawsuit against AI music generator
mbw-wmg-suno.support: Trade report quoting the companies' release: partnership and settlement, licensed models in 2026, downloads need a paid account.

mbw-kobalt-udio.title: After Universal, Warner, and Merlin deals, now Udio inks licensing agreement with Kobalt
mbw-kobalt-udio.support: Trade report of the 9 Apr 2026 Kobalt deal; opt-in voices and compositions; platform expected later in 2026.

gema-licensing.title: Two components, one goal: music creators shall receive fair shares through effective AI licensing
gema-licensing.support: Two component licensing model: 30% of net income, minimum royalty tied to output, German-market providers; second component for later use of AI music.

cisac-stim.title: STIM launches world's first collective AI music licence
cisac-stim.support: Society news: licence with Songfox and Sureel attribution; open framework; deliberately limited repertoire at launch.

socan-musical-ai.title: SOCAN announces collaboration with Musical AI to advance music creator attribution, remuneration and transparency in AI
socan-musical-ai.support: Release: approved technology partner for attribution; opt-in and credit-and-compensation principles; no rates or payout mechanics stated.

deezer-2026-07.title: Deezer: AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time
deezer-2026-07.support: Deezer's own figures: over 50% of daily uploads at June 2026 peak, about 90,000 a day, 1 to 3% of streams, up to 85% fraud in 2025. Gives June 2025 and June 2026 for its first AI tagging.

youtube-altered-content.title: Disclosing use of GenAI content
youtube-altered-content.support: Help page: creators must disclose realistic AI-made or meaningfully altered content, including music that is the main focus of a video; labels; possible penalties for repeated non-disclosure.

youtube-likeness-blog.title: Expanding likeness detection to the entertainment industry
youtube-likeness-blog.support: Blog post: likeness detection offered to talent agencies, management companies and the people they represent; describes face matching.

mbw-apple-tags.title: Apple Music launches AI transparency tags, but only if labels and distributors declare them
mbw-apple-tags.support: Trade report of Apple's 4 Mar 2026 partner newsletter: four tags, supplier-declared, required for new deliveries later.

cdbaby-spotify-ai.title: What to know about Spotify's new AI protections
cdbaby-spotify-ai.support: CD Baby's own post (by Ryan DiLello): it is working with Spotify and partners on an industry standard for AI credits in track metadata, and on stopping uploads to the wrong artist profile.

ddex-ern-part1.title: Electronic Release Notification Message Suite, Part 1: Definitions of Messages (release notes)
ddex-ern-part1.support: Annex A release notes: version 4.3.1 adds communication that a recording, and a contribution, was made fully or partly by a generative AI tool.

socan-alignment.title: ASCAP, BMI and SOCAN announce alignment on AI registration policies
socan-alignment.support: Three societies accept partially AI-generated works; entirely AI-created works are not eligible.

socan-suno-claim.publisher: Plaintiff SOCAN (filed in the Federal Court of Canada)
socan-suno-claim.title: Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Suno, Inc., Amended Statement of Claim
socan-suno-claim.support: Court File No. T-3803-26, Federal Court; claim issued 2 Sep 2026, amended 18 Nov 2026 under Rule 200; alleges infringement of SOCAN's performing rights in listed works. Allegations only.

eu-2026-1744.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal of the EU)
eu-2026-1744.title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
eu-2026-1744.support: Point (39)(b) adds Art. 111(4) to the AI Act: providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 must comply with Art. 50(2) by 2 Dec 2026. OJ L 24.7.2026; in force on the third day.
